title: Concerning Things for Which Men, and Especially Princes, Are Praised or Blamed
hook: The praise scroll looks warm until the grain-depth rod touches winter.
counterintuition: The mistake is to keep a praised quality even when it helps ruin the state. The better move is to test every virtue and vice label against real conditions and necessity.
tryThisNow: Choose one praised quality in a political crisis. Write when using it preserves the state, then when insisting on it would help ruin the state.
keyTakeaway: A ruler should judge praised and blamed qualities by preservation: avoid vices that lose the state, and accept reproach when necessity leaves no safer course.

breakdown.fastRead: A famine regent lays a court praise scroll under the grain-depth rod. The poets call her generous. The granary says the city will not survive winter if she keeps the admired distribution. Real truth begins there: with what the action does, not what the label flatters. A quality that looks like virtue can ruin the state. A blamed act can preserve it. The test is not which word sounds clean. The test is what keeps the state alive under real conditions.
breakdown.deepRead:
A ruler is praised and blamed through labels: generous or miserly, merciful or cruel, faithful or faithless, easy or hard, sincere or cunning. The trap is to treat the good-sounding word as the answer before asking what the situation demands. Human conditions do not let a prince hold every praised quality at all times among people who do not live that way.

A besieged port judge touches a mercy petition while smugglers sell powder to enemy boats. His compassion is admired. Then he opens the powder-bin tally and sees how close the harbor guns are to silence. If he keeps strict mercy now, the blockade defense breaks. He signs the hard sentence only after the empty bin shows what compassion would cost.

This is not a worship of vice. It is a test of necessity. The ruler should avoid the reproach of acts that would cost him the state. If possible, he should avoid lesser reproaches too. But if the state can scarcely be saved without an act that draws blame, he should not treat the clean label as more sacred than preservation.

The real truth is harsher than the imagined picture because actions have consequences beyond reputation. Mercy, openness, faith, ease, and affability may preserve order in one setting and endanger it in another. The practical question is not whether the word is praised. The question is whether this use of the quality preserves or ruins the state.
breakdown.fullRead:
A broken ferry chain lies across a treaty clause in the council room at midnight. Levan, a minor prince, reads his oath aloud because keeping perfect faith has always been his proudest quality. Then he places the enemy's broken chain on the clause. The other side has already cut the ferry and seized boats near the last river crossing. He asks whether virtue still names the same action when one party has turned the promise into a weapon.

The move is to leave imagined rule and follow the real truth of the matter. In imagined rule, every praised quality can be held together: generosity without shortage, mercy without danger, faith without betrayal, openness without infiltration. In real rule, qualities collide with conditions. The ruler must decide under scarcity, fear, treachery, armed pressure, disease, and human ambition.

That does not make labels useless. Praise and blame still matter because people judge rulers through them. A prince called rapacious, cruel, faithless, cowardly, or frivolous may lose support and invite danger. The point is more exact: some vices lose the state and must be avoided. Other reproaches may have to be borne when avoiding them would make preservation almost impossible.

A frontier council learns this with public openness. Beren and the councillors are proud of publishing every gate watch list. Before the next proclamation is posted, the watch captain lays a captured route sketch over it. The overlap shows enemy infiltrators were using the admired transparency as a road map. Openness still sounds noble. In that moment, publishing patrol routes would serve the enemy more than the city.

A restored ruler faces the same test from a different label. Sava wants to be called easy after years of exile. In the barracks, a captain says the unpaid men will like him better if he waives the muster. Sava taps the empty muster peg and asks which reputation leaves him with a state tomorrow. Ease may look humane in calm days. Before armed men testing command, it can teach them that orders are negotiable.

A plague border commander makes the limit plain. Noor's postmortem sets the merchants' compliment note beside the fever mark on the inspection slate. Pleasant speed would have won praise at the cordon rope. The hated delay kept infection out of the capital. The blamed action preserved what the praised shortcut risked.

Use this judgment carefully. A ruler who enjoys blame has missed the point. A ruler who calls every convenience necessity has missed it too. Necessity must be tied to preservation, not appetite. The hard act needs a real condition: a powder bin emptying, a broken treaty chain, a route sketch in enemy hands, a fever mark near the gate.

The final test is concrete. Ask what the praised action will do here. Ask what the blamed action will prevent here. Avoid the vices that would lose the state. Do not cling to a clean word when the clean word carries ruin inside it.

examples.title: Catrin Sets Praise Under the Rod

planSpec.domain: a famine regent choosing whether to keep the praised title of generous distributor after stores fall below winter survival levels
planSpec.audience: a ruler whose court poets praise openhandedness while granary stewards show ruin approaching
planSpec.stakes: continuing the admired distribution wins praise now and destroys the state before thaw
planSpec.requiredBeat: The regent sets the praise scroll under the grain-depth rod and orders the ration cut because the rod, not the compliment, tells whether the city survives.

examples.scenario: A grain-depth rod rests across a court praise scroll in the north granary at 6:10 a.m. Catrin, famine regent of the river capital, must decide whether to keep the praised title of generous distributor after stores fall below winter survival levels. She sets the scroll under the rod and signs the winter ration order because the rod, not the compliment, tells whether the city survives.
examples.whatToDo: Let the survival measure outrank the praise. Catrin should cut rations now because openhanded distribution would empty the granary before thaw.
examples.whyItMatters: Generosity keeps its good name only if the state can live with it. Here the praised habit would turn admiration into winter ruin.

examples.title: Jovan Opens the Powder Tally

planSpec.domain: a besieged port judge deciding whether strict mercy toward smugglers will collapse the blockade defense
planSpec.audience: a judge praised for compassion who now faces crews selling powder to enemy boats
planSpec.stakes: mercy keeps his reputation clean but lets the harbor guns go silent
planSpec.requiredBeat: He touches the mercy petition, then opens the powder-bin tally and signs the hard sentence only after the empty bin shows what compassion would cost.

examples.scenario: A mercy petition lies beside an open powder-bin tally in the port court at 9:45 p.m. Jovan, judge of the besieged harbor, must decide whether compassion toward captured smugglers still preserves the city. He touches the petition, opens the tally, and signs the hard sentence only after the empty bin shows what mercy would cost the harbor guns.
examples.whatToDo: Tie mercy to the blockade's survival. Jovan should judge the smugglers by the powder loss before protecting his compassionate reputation.
examples.whyItMatters: A clean reputation cannot fire silent guns. If mercy lets crews sell powder to enemy boats, the praised quality becomes a path to defeat.

examples.title: Levan Places the Broken Chain

planSpec.domain: a treaty council where a minor prince must decide whether perfect faith with a broken partner will surrender his last river crossing
planSpec.audience: a ruler trained to prize keeping every promise as an absolute virtue
planSpec.stakes: observing the treaty after the other side has already violated it would hand over the crossing that keeps the state alive
planSpec.requiredBeat: The prince reads his oath aloud, then places the enemy's broken ferry chain on the treaty clause and asks whether virtue still names the same action.

examples.scenario: A broken ferry chain lies across a treaty clause in the west council room at 12:05 a.m. Levan, minor prince of the upper ford, must decide whether perfect faith with a broken partner will surrender his last river crossing. He predicts his advisers will urge obedience, reads his oath aloud, then places the enemy's chain on the clause and asks whether virtue still names the same action.
examples.whatToDo: Test faith against the broken condition. Levan should not surrender the last crossing under a treaty the other side has already turned against him.
examples.whyItMatters: Keeping faith with a broken partner can become surrender, not virtue. The crossing is the state's life, and the chain shows the old condition is gone.

examples.title: Beren Sees the Route Overlap

planSpec.domain: a frontier city council praised for openness deciding whether to publish patrol routes during infiltration scares
planSpec.audience: councillors who fear being called secretive more than they fear losing the gates
planSpec.stakes: the admired habit of public disclosure can become the road map for enemies inside the city
planSpec.requiredBeat: Before the notice is posted, the watch captain lays a captured route sketch over the transparency proclamation and waits until the councillors see the overlap.

examples.scenario: A captured route sketch covers half of a transparency proclamation in the frontier city records hall at 2:20 p.m. Before the patrol notice is posted, Councillor Beren praises the city's open gate watch list. The watch captain lays the enemy sketch over the proclamation and waits until Beren sees the overlap with tomorrow's routes.
examples.whatToDo: Withhold the patrol routes while infiltration is active. Beren should protect the gate watch list instead of preserving a public image of total openness.
examples.whyItMatters: Disclosure can preserve trust in calm times and endanger gates during infiltration. Here openness gives enemies the road map they need.

examples.title: Sava Taps the Empty Muster Peg

planSpec.domain: a newly restored ruler deciding whether to preserve a reputation for ease while unpaid soldiers test command
planSpec.audience: a prince who wants to be called gentle after years of exile
planSpec.stakes: ease looks humane in calm days but teaches armed men that orders can be negotiated away
planSpec.requiredBeat: When the captain says the men will like him better if he waives the muster, the ruler taps the empty muster peg and asks which reputation leaves him with a state tomorrow.

examples.scenario: An empty muster peg sticks out from a barracks wall beside the returned ruler's cloak at 7:00 a.m. Sava, newly restored ruler of the hill state, must decide whether to waive muster for unpaid soldiers. "They will like you better," the captain says, holding the request. Sava taps the empty peg. "Which reputation leaves me with a state tomorrow?"
examples.whatToDo: Hold the muster. Sava should prefer the blamed firmness that keeps command over the praised ease that teaches armed men to bargain away orders.
examples.whyItMatters: Ease can look humane until soldiers test whether command exists. A gentle reputation is useless if it leaves the restored state without obedience.

examples.title: Noor Sets the Compliment Beside Fever

planSpec.domain: a plague border station where a commander must choose between affability to merchants and hated inspection delays
planSpec.audience: a commander blamed as harsh by traders waiting outside the cordon
planSpec.stakes: pleasant speed would be praised at the gate and may carry disease into the capital
planSpec.requiredBeat: The commander places the merchants' compliment note beside the fever mark on the inspection slate and shows why the blamed delay preserved what the praised shortcut risked.

examples.scenario: A fever mark is circled on an inspection slate beside a merchants' compliment note at the north cordon station at 4:35 p.m. Noor, commander of the plague border post, writes the postmortem after traders curse the delays. She places the compliment beside the fever mark and shows why the blamed delay preserved what the praised shortcut risked.
examples.whatToDo: Defend the inspection delay with evidence. Noor should accept blame for harshness when pleasant speed would carry fever through the cordon rope.
examples.whyItMatters: Affability would win praise at the gate and risk disease in the capital. The delay is blamed, but it preserves what the shortcut endangers.

questions.prompt: A famine regent is praised for openhanded grain distribution. The grain-depth rod shows the city will not survive winter at that rate. What should she do?
choices: Keep the praised distribution because reputation matters more than stores.
Cut the ration because preservation outranks the praise label in this condition.
Empty the granary faster so people see her generosity before thaw.
questions.explanation: The rod shows what the compliment hides. Generosity is praised, but under winter scarcity the same habit would help ruin the city.

questions.prompt: A port judge is known for mercy. During a blockade, smugglers sell powder to enemy boats and the harbor gun bins are almost empty. Which judgment fits the real pressure?
choices: Mercy should be automatic because it is praised.
Punishment is admirable whenever it frightens people.
A hard sentence may be necessary because mercy would silence the guns.
questions.explanation: The point is not to admire punishment. The powder-bin tally ties the hard sentence to preservation of the blockade defense.

questions.prompt: A treaty partner cuts the ferry chain first, then demands that a minor prince keep the clause that surrenders his last river crossing. What is the prince's best analysis?
choices: Perfect faith may no longer name the same action once the other side has broken the condition.
Every broken treaty gives permission for any act the prince wants.
The prince must keep the clause because keeping promises is always praised.
questions.explanation: The broken chain changes the condition. Refusing surrender of the last crossing is tied to preservation, not to a general license to do anything.

questions.prompt: A frontier council is praised for publishing patrol routes. A captured enemy sketch matches tomorrow's gate watch list. What should the council see?
choices: Openness still preserves the city because it sounds virtuous.
The admired disclosure has become useful to infiltrators.
Secrecy is always better than public trust.
questions.explanation: The overlap is the test. Public disclosure can build trust, but here it gives enemies a route map, so the praised habit endangers the gates.

questions.prompt: A restored ruler wants to be called easy and gentle. Unpaid soldiers ask him to waive the first muster, and the barracks peg is empty. What is at stake?
choices: Whether ease teaches armed men that command can be negotiated away.
Whether all gentle conduct must be rejected forever.
Whether soldiers should be praised more often.
questions.explanation: The empty peg makes the issue concrete. Ease may look humane, but before armed men testing command it can weaken the restored state.

questions.prompt: At a plague border station, merchants praise quick passage. The inspection slate shows a fever mark near their caravan. What should the commander choose?
choices: Quick passage because affability is a praised quality.
A delay tied to the fever evidence, even if traders call it harsh.
Permanent closure of every gate because blame no longer matters.
questions.explanation: The fever mark supplies necessity. The delay is not harshness for its own sake; it preserves the capital from what pleasant speed risks.

questions.prompt: A ruler hears a courtier say, "Any vice is acceptable if it helps me today." What correction follows the preservation test?
choices: Only accept blame where necessity ties the act to saving the state.
Vice is always stronger than virtue.
Praised conduct should be avoided because it is naive.
questions.explanation: The test is stricter than convenience. A blamed act needs a real necessity connected to preservation, not the ruler's appetite or short-term comfort.

questions.prompt: In a captured border town at 11:00 p.m., a prince refuses to alter any praised conduct even after rival captains break safe-conducts and seize supplies. "I will follow every virtue exactly," he says. What danger does he miss?
choices: He misses that enemies will always become virtuous if he waits.
He misses that virtue labels do not apply to rulers.
He may ruin himself among people who do not act by the same professions.
questions.explanation: The danger is not that virtues are meaningless. The danger is insisting on every praised conduct when real conditions and other actors make that ruinous.

questions.prompt: A council compares two options: one looks compassionate but leaves the city defenseless, the other looks severe but keeps the city alive. What should decide?
choices: The label that will sound best in songs.
The action's effect on preservation under the actual conditions.
The option that creates the strongest fear regardless of facts.
questions.explanation: Praise and blame are not enough by themselves. The council must ask which action preserves the state under the pressure in front of it.

reviewCards.front: A praised quality would empty the winter granary. What question should come first?
reviewCards.back: Ask what the action does under real conditions. A good label cannot save a city if the act itself moves the state toward ruin.

reviewCards.front: A hard sentence is blamed, but powder is being sold to enemy boats. How should you test it?
reviewCards.back: Tie the blamed act to necessity. If it preserves the harbor guns and avoids collapse, the reproach may have to be borne.

reviewCards.front: Someone says the lesson is that vice is admirable. What is the correction?
reviewCards.back: Vice is not admirable by itself. The test is preservation: avoid vices that lose the state and accept reproach only where necessity requires it.

reviewCards.front: A treaty partner breaks the ferry chain first. What changes in judging perfect faith?
reviewCards.back: The condition has changed. Keeping the same clause may no longer preserve faith; it may surrender the last crossing that keeps the state alive.

reviewCards.front: A council fears being called secretive if it withholds patrol routes. What evidence matters?
reviewCards.back: The captured route sketch matters. If openness gives enemies a map, the praised label must yield to preservation.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Test praise and blame against preservation. Do not ask first whether a label sounds virtuous or vicious; ask what the action does under the real pressure facing the state.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a praised habit consumes what the state needs to survive, then measure the supply first and let the label wait.
If an action draws reproach, then name the concrete danger it prevents before calling it necessary.
If a partner violates the condition of a promise, then retest whether keeping the same promise still preserves the state.
If fear of a bad name drives the decision, then place the reputation beside the material evidence of preservation or ruin.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one praised quality in a real political crisis and write two conditions: when using it preserves the state, and when insisting on it helps ruin the state.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, collect three public praise or blame labels from political news. For each one, write the action's likely effect on preservation, not just the label's moral sound.

memorableLines.text: The test is not which word sounds clean.
memorableLines.why: It blocks the easy move of judging by reputation alone.

memorableLines.text: A ruler who enjoys blame has missed the point.
memorableLines.why: It keeps the chapter from sliding into vice admiration.

memorableLines.text: Do not cling to a clean word when the clean word carries ruin inside it.
memorableLines.why: It makes the preservation test memorable and concrete.
